name: llama_index

facts.description: LlamaIndex is the document processing platform for AI

title: LlamaIndex: The Document Processing Platform for AI Applications
answer: LlamaIndex is an open source Python framework, maintained by run-llama under the MIT licence, for connecting large language models to your own data. It handles document parsing, indexing, retrieval, agents and structured extraction, and it sits between raw data sources and the model layer. The one thing to know before adopting it is that its centre of gravity has shifted toward LlamaParse and LlamaCloud, so some of the most polished document processing is a hosted product rather than purely local library code.

sections.body: LlamaIndex is made by run-llama and distributed as an open source Python library under the MIT licence, with its repository at github.com/run-llama/llama_index. The site describes it plainly as the document processing platform for AI. It appeared as a data framework for LLM applications and now spans several layers of the stack: ingestion and parsing of documents, indexing and vector storage, retrieval engines, graph construction, agent workflows and model integrations. In a typical architecture it sits between your raw data and the model provider, supplying the context that a model alone cannot see. The core package is llama-index-core, and the LLM class documented there is described as the main class for interacting with language models.
sections.heading: What it is and where it sits in AI work

sections.body: The concrete jobs the documentation shows are broad. On the data side there is document parsing, chunking with SentenceSplitter, embedding and vector storage, with integrations such as VertexAIVectorStore and VertexTextEmbedding. On the retrieval side there are query engines, GraphRAG pipelines that extract entities and relationships, build communities with hierarchical Leiden and summarise them for global answers, and a GraphQueryEngine that consolidates intermediate answers. On the model side there are LLM integrations including Cloudflare AI Gateway for fallback and load balancing across providers, and Baseten for dedicated or model APIs endpoints. There is also agent and tool calling support, structured prediction, streaming, and fine-tuning examples such as distilling a GPT-4 pairwise judge into GPT-3.5. It is strongest where you need to connect many document types and many model providers through one interface, and where graph or hierarchical retrieval over a corpus matters more than raw inference speed.
sections.heading: What it is used for and where it is strongest

sections.body: The learning curve is moderate. You need working Python, and for the retrieval and graph material some familiarity with embeddings, vector search and the idea of chunking helps considerably. The GraphRAG example assumes you can follow entity and relationship extraction, community detection and summarisation, and it asks for a Google Cloud project with the Vertex AI API enabled. Mathematics is not a hard prerequisite for ordinary use, though understanding similarity and ranking makes the retrieval behaviour less mysterious. The official site offers a large body of API reference pages and notebook examples, including complete install commands and runnable cookbooks, which is a reasonable starting point for a beginner who already knows Python. The material is reference-heavy rather than tutorial-shaped in places, so expect to read code as much as prose.
sections.heading: How hard it is to learn and what you need first

sections.body: The ecosystem is the framework's main asset. The site documents integrations across model providers and infrastructure, including Cloudflare AI Gateway, Baseten, Vertex AI, Azure, and gateways such as Bifrost, Portkey and LiteLLM for self-hosted LlamaCloud. There are separate integration packages, for example llama-index-llms-baseten and llama-index-vector-stores-vertexaivectorsearch, alongside the core. Documentation covers API references, examples and cookbooks, and self-hosting configuration for LlamaParse and LlamaCloud. The repository has roughly fifty two thousand stars, which indicates a large and active user base, and the last recorded push was in October 2026. Community support is therefore substantial, though the documentation is spread across framework reference, examples and product pages rather than gathered in one place.
sections.heading: Ecosystem and community

sections.body: LlamaIndex is built for both, but with different costs. Prototyping is fast because a reader can wire a reader, a splitter, an embedding model and a query engine together in a few lines, and the examples show exactly that. Production use is supported through explicit control: chunk sizes and overlaps, model ordering and fallback, priority and tags for parsing tiers, retries and timeouts, custom endpoints and headers, and separate sync and async paths. The Cloudflare AI Gateway integration, for instance, exposes max_retries defaulting to 3 and a timeout defaulting to 60 seconds, and Baseten documents that async completion requires a webhook endpoint and is not supported with model APIs endpoints. The cost of that flexibility is configuration surface, and some features, such as binding support in the Cloudflare gateway class, are documented as not yet implemented.
sections.heading: Prototyping speed against production performance

sections.body: The facts and the site support a picture of a widely used, current framework rather than a legacy one. The repository carries over fifty thousand stars, the project is actively pushed, and the documentation covers enterprise concerns such as self-hosted and BYOC deployments, Azure and Vertex authentication, managed embeddings and tiered parsing fallback. That suggests adoption in teams building retrieval and document processing products, and skills in it transfer to work on RAG systems, agents and data pipelines. What the material does not provide is any named customer list, deployment count or survey of market share, so claims about being the standard in any particular industry would go beyond what is documented here. For someone choosing what to learn, it is a reasonable bet alongside, not instead of, general Python and model serving skills.
sections.heading: Industry adoption and careers

sections.body: LlamaIndex is a Python framework, and the site's examples are Python throughout, with pip install commands and imports from llama_index packages. It is typically used with model providers such as OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, Vertex AI serving Gemini and Claude, Baseten, and gateways that front several providers. It is used with vector stores, including Vertex AI Vector Search, and with graph tooling such as graspologic for hierarchical Leiden community detection. It also appears alongside HuggingFace models in the fine-tuning examples. The polyglot pattern it belongs to is the common one where Python handles data preparation, retrieval and orchestration, while the model itself may be served anywhere, and other languages call into the resulting service rather than reimplementing the framework.
sections.heading: How it fits beside the others

sections.body: Several limits are visible in the documentation itself. Binding support in the Cloudflare AI Gateway class raises NotImplementedError, so that path is incomplete. Output parsing is not supported for streaming, and async operations are not supported with Baseten model APIs endpoints. In the GraphRAG example, only relationship descriptions are used in the current implementation, with entity descriptions promised for a later retrieval stage. Provider configuration does not guarantee upstream availability, since the account, region, deployment or gateway must still be configured, and a model only runs when credentials validate at startup. The official material does not state benchmark performance, memory overhead, or how the hosted LlamaParse and LlamaCloud products compare with the open source library for cost or data residency, so those questions remain open.
sections.heading: Limits and open questions
